topic: Life appeared on Earth by at least 3.5 billion years ago, possibly by 3.7; all living things descend from a common ancestor.
For about two billion years life was single-celled; eukaryotes, then multicellular life, followed.
Animals diversified in the Cambrian explosion about 538 million years ago; plants and animals colonised land from about 470 million years ago.
Mass extinctions repeatedly cleared the way for new groups: dinosaurs after the Permian–Triassic extinction, mammals after the Cretaceous–Paleogene.

Earliest history of Earth: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago; the Moon probably formed when a Mars-sized body, Theia, struck it.
Liquid water existed by about 4.4 billion years ago, judging from zircon crystals.
Early Earth was bombarded by asteroids and comets, which may have delivered water and organic compounds.
Earliest evidence for life on Earth: The oldest undisputed fossils, of bacteria, are about 3 billion years old; disputed finds go back to 3.5 billion years and more.
Stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, are among the oldest fossils.
Carbon isotope signatures in rocks from Greenland suggest life by 3.7–3.8 billion years ago.
Origins of life on Earth: All organisms share a last universal common ancestor (LUCA), since their core biochemistry is shared.
Theories differ on what came first: self-copying RNA (the RNA world), a metabolism on mineral surfaces (iron–sulfur world), or membranes (lipid world).
Candidate birthplaces include deep-sea hydrothermal vents and land-based hot springs.
Panspermia holds that life was seeded from space; it moves the question rather than answering it.
Environmental and evolutionary impact of: Microbial mats are thin, layered colonies of microbes, each layer feeding on the by-products of the next.
Cyanobacteria in the mats invented oxygen-producing photosynthesis.
Their oxygen, building up from about 2.4 billion years ago (the Great Oxygenation Event), transformed the atmosphere and made complex life possible.
Diversification of eukaryotes: Eukaryotes are cells with a nucleus and internal compartments; they appear in the fossil record about 1.8–2 billion years ago.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria engulfed by other cells (endosymbiosis).
Most eukaryotes use oxygen, which their mitochondria burn to make energy.
Sexual reproduction and multicellular or: Sexual reproduction (meiosis and fertilisation) mixes genes; it evolved in early eukaryotes, perhaps 1.2 billion years ago or more.
Multicellularity evolved independently many times, in animals, plants, fungi and algae.
The Ediacaran biota, 580–539 million years ago, were the first large, complex multicellular organisms.
Emergence of animals: Animals are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; all but sponges have tissues such as muscle and nerves.
In the Cambrian explosion, from about 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appeared within some 20 million years.
Fossil beds such as the Burgess Shale preserve soft-bodied Cambrian animals.
The first chordates and vertebrates (jawless fish) appeared in the Cambrian.
Evolution of terrestrial antioxidants: Life on land had to solve drying out, supporting weight against gravity, breathing air and reproducing without water.
Land plants and animals evolved antioxidants to cope with stronger sunlight and more oxygen.
Plants were on land by about 470 million years ago, in the Ordovician.
Evolution of soil: Before life colonised land there was no soil, only bare rock and sand.
Lichens, microbes and early plants broke down rock and added organic matter, building the first soils.
Plant roots in the Devonian deepened soils and sped up rock weathering.
Plants and the Late Devonian wood crisis: Land plants evolved vascular tissue to carry water, and later roots, leaves, wood and seeds.
The first trees and forests arose in the Devonian, about 385 million years ago.
By drawing down carbon dioxide and releasing nutrients into the sea, they may have helped cause the Late Devonian extinction.
Land invertebrates: Arthropods, such as early myriapods and arachnids, were among the first land animals, in the Silurian and Devonian.
Land animals evolved internal fertilisation, new eyes for air, and in many cases hearing.
Insects appeared by the Devonian and became the first animals to fly, in the Carboniferous.
Amphibians: Tetrapods (four-limbed vertebrates) evolved from lobe-finned fish in the Late Devonian, 370–360 million years ago.
Early forms such as Acanthostega had limbs but still lived mainly in water.
Amphibians keep an aquatic larval stage (tadpoles); they dominated land until the Carboniferous rainforest collapse.
Reptiles: Amniotes, whose eggs survive on dry land, evolved in the Late Carboniferous.
They split into synapsids (the line to mammals) and sauropsids (reptiles and birds) about 313 million years ago.
Synapsids dominated the Permian; after the end-Permian extinction, archosaurs, including dinosaurs, took over.
Birds: Birds evolved from small, feathered theropod dinosaurs in the Late Jurassic; Archaeopteryx is an early example.
Early birds had teeth and long bony tails; beaks and short tails followed.
Birds are the only dinosaurs that survived the extinction 66 million years ago.
Mammals: Mammals descend from therapsids, synapsids that survived the end-Permian extinction.
Early mammals were small, mostly nocturnal insectivores living alongside dinosaurs; nocturnal life may have favoured warm blood and fur.
After the dinosaurs' extinction, mammals diversified into most of today's groups.
Flowering plants: Flowering plants (angiosperms) appeared about 130 million years ago and diversified rapidly in the Cretaceous.
Their rise went hand in hand with pollinating insects.
With about 300,000 species, they now dominate most land vegetation.
Social insects: In eusocial insects (ants, bees, termites, wasps), most colony members are sterile workers.
Eusociality has evolved independently only about a dozen times among arthropods.
Kin selection explains it: helping close relatives breed passes on shared genes.
Humans: Robert Chambers in 1844 and Charles Darwin in 1871 proposed that humans evolved from a common ancestor with other animals.
The human line split from the chimpanzee line about 6–7 million years ago; Sahelanthropus is a very early member.
The first known stone tools were made about 2.6 million years ago; modern humans appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
Mass extinctions: Life has suffered at least five mass extinctions in the last 540 million years.
Extinctions remove dominant groups and open niches for others: mammals spread after the dinosaurs died out.
The end-Permian extinction, 252 million years ago, was the largest; the end-Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, was caused by an asteroid impact.
